content:Speaker user says: Is there a way to set up a separate feed or sidebar on Twitter that displays recommended content based on my interests and the people I follow, without having to sift through retweets and duplicate content?: March 2016 – Things I think.
I just went through my entire list of people I was following on Twitter and cleaned house. Even though my following count was only just over 100, I’ve begun to really dislike scrolling through my feed without having gained any useful knowledge. Did I really need to spend those few minutes looking at my feed? Did I gain anything of value besides finding a way to spend a few minutes (minimum) of my life?
In deciding who to unfollow, there were so many people that I thought were interesting but didn’t necessarily publish content on a day to day basis that I was interested in. There’s so much duplication of content that I need to sift through when scrolling through my feed. I love baseball and so I follow a lot of baseball related accounts, but that doesn’t necessarily mean that I want to see a majority of baseball content in my feed- it just means I want to see a variety of baseball content/sources in my feed. I ended up creating a baseball list devoted to baseball accounts that I followed. Now if I want to hear some baseball stuff, I’ll have to search the dark corners of Twitter to get to said baseball list; Seriously Twitter, why even have a Lists feature if it’s so hard to access?
The same is true for politics: I might follow a few Bernie Sanders related accounts but I don’t want to be bombarded with a Bernie tweet ever 15 minutes. I might just be following them because I think he’s an interesting guy and want some Bernie related content. Some people publish rich original content occasionally that I don’t want to miss out on, but I don’t want to have the added cost of having to sift through the remainder of what they publish.
A separate feed or sidebar that contains content either retweeted by people I follow, or recommended content based on who I follow and what I like. It’s interesting that some accounts with the most interesting content often retweet other interesting content, which I may also appreciate. Ltd, Pune-based visual collaboration platform Framebench, in-app customer support platform Konotor, social recommendations platform Frilp, and video chat software 1Click.io.

content:Speaker assistant says: Software testing compatibility with hardware is crucial to ensure proper functioning of the software on the particular hardware platform. It is essential because:

1. Ensures proper functioning: Compatibility testing ensures that the software works seamlessly on the hardware platform it is intended for. It helps to identify any issues that may arise due to system configuration variation, hardware or software component changes, or any other compatibility issues between software and hardware.

2. Avoids software crashes: Compatibility issues between software and hardware can result in system crashes, data loss, and other severe issues. Thorough testing of compatibility can prevent these problems, which can lead to improved user experience, trust, and customer loyalty.

3. Cost-effective: Compatibility testing at an early stage can save a lot of time and money by detecting compatibility issues before it reaches the end-user. Resolving issues post-deployment can be time-consuming, expensive, and can adversely affect the user's trust in the software.

4. Improves market share: Compatibility testing ensures that the software functions properly on a wide range of hardware platforms, and this results in an increased user base, leading to more revenue and better market share.

In conclusion, software testing compatibility with hardware is critical for software's success. It ensures better user experience, avoids software crashes, saves time and money, and improves the software's market position. context:Windows keywords: software, compatibility, hardware, testing, software tags: multitasking

content:Speaker user says: Hey, thanks for explaining the importance of software testing compatibility with hardware. Can you add some more information on how compatibility testing can affect the software's performance? And what factors should be considered during compatibility testing? context:431 keywords: software testing, compatibility, performance, hardware tags: hardware, operating systems, third-party applications, database, software development

content:Speaker assistant says: Sure, let me explain.

How compatibility testing can affect the software's performance:

1. Hardware Configuration: Compatibility testing ensures that the software behaves in the same way across a range of hardware types and configurations. If the software is not compatible with some particular hardware, it may result in poor performance, latency, or crashes.

2. Operating System Versions: Compatibility testing for different operating systems is necessary as different operating systems have different APIs that can impact the software behavior. A change in the operating system version can cause compatibility issues like different graphics drivers, disk drivers, and other dependencies that may impact the software's performance.

3. Web Browser Compatibility: Websites and web-based applications must undergo compatibility testing for various browsers to ensure cross-browser compatibility. Web applications function and look differently on different browsers, and compatibility testing helps identify any issues and fix them.

Factors to be considered during compatibility testing:

1. Supported Hardware: The software compatibility testing should be performed on a range of hardware types, including different configurations, from different manufacturers.

2. Operating System: Compatibility testing should be carried out on various operating systems that support the software.

3. Third-party applications: It is crucial to check the compatibility of the software with other related applications that run on the same system.

4. Database Compatibility: Compatibility testing should be performed with different databases that are required for the software.

5. Documentation: It is essential to document all the test cases and results to ensure that compatibility testing has been carried out rigorously.

In conclusion, compatibility testing is vital to delivering high-quality software that performs well across various hardware and software configurations. It ensures that the software works seamlessly on the intended platform, minimizing risks, and improving user experience. context:Switch-It keywords: compatibility, software, hardware, operating systems, compatibility testing tags: software, hardware, compatibility, performance, testing

content:Speaker user says: Hey, great explanation! Can you also provide some examples of compatibility issues that can arise between software and hardware during testing? I want to have a better understanding of this issue. context:432 keywords: software, hardware, compatibility, issues, examples tags: software compatibility, hardware compatibility, testing, performance, user experience

content:Speaker assistant says: Sure, here are some examples of compatibility issues that can arise between software and hardware during testing:

1. Driver Compatibility: One of the most common compatibility issues is the inability of the software to recognize drivers installed on a computer system. Sometimes, software may not have the correct drivers that are required to run on a particular hardware platform.

2. Memory Compatibility: Different hardware have different memory configurations. Compatibility issues can arise when software is unable to allocate and manage its memory on a specific system, resulting in poor performance and crashes.

3. Processor Compatibility: Some software may not run optimally on specific processors, which can lead to software crashes, system hangs, and other performance-related issues.

4. Peripheral Compatibility: Compatibility issues can arise with peripherals like printers, scanners, or cameras. The software may not recognize or function correctly with the specific hardware, leading to unexpected behavior or system crashes.

5. Operating System Compatibility: Software must be compatible with different operating systems as each OS varies in its architecture, functionality, and feature set. Incompatibility with the operating system can result in installation errors, conflicts with other installed software, or system crashes.

In conclusion, compatibility issues can arise due to various hardware configurations and software requirements. Therefore, it is essential to perform compatibility testing to identify these issues before software deployment, resolving them, and ensuring software runs smoothly on different hardware and software configurations. context:This text outlines common compatibility problems encountered when software interacts with hardware, including driver issues, memory limitations, processor conflicts, peripheral malfunctions, and operating system differences. keywords: software, hardware, compatibility, issues tags: Software Compatibility, Hardware Compatibility, System Testing

1. BrowserStack: This tool is useful for testing websites and web applications for cross-browser compatibility. You can check your software's functionality and appearance on different browsers and versions, including legacy versions.

2. Sauce Labs: Sauce Labs is a cloud-based platform that provides virtual machines to test compatibility across different operating systems, browsers, and devices. 3. Speedster: Speedster is a tool used for testing software performance on different hardware configurations. With Speedster, you can compare the performance and responsiveness of your software on different hardware, including laptops, desktops, and servers.

4. InstallShield: InstallShield is a software installation development tool that enables developers to create installers that are compatible with different operating systems and hardware configurations. It can help to verify the compatibility of the software installer with various configurations.

5. VMWare and VirtualBox: VMWare and VirtualBox allow you to create virtual machines to test software compatibility. These tools allow you to simulate different hardware and operating system environments to test compatibility with your software.

content:Speaker assistant says: Certainly, here are some methods used to perform compatibility testing:

1. Manual Testing: Manual testing involves having a tester use the software on different hardware platforms, operating systems, and browsers to verify compatibility. It involves running a set of test cases and using the software in a real-world scenario. This method is time-consuming, but it helps to find issues that automated tools might miss. 2. Automated Testing: Automated testing involves using specialized tools to test software on different hardware, browsers, and operating system configurations. The tests are automated, which means they can efficiently execute large test suites quickly, and can also help to identify bugs and other issues faster. 3. Virtualization: Virtualization tools allow developers to create virtual machines that mimic different hardware configurations, operating systems, and browser environments. Developers can use virtual environments to test the application on various configurations, minimizing the need for physical devices. 4. Cloud-Based Testing: Cloud-based testing is a newer approach to testing that utilizes cloud computing. Software applications are deployed on a cloud system that simulates different configurations, enabling the software to be tested using real-world scenarios. 5. Beta Testing: Beta testing involves releasing the software to a group of beta testers who use the software in real-world scenarios on different hardware and software configurations. This method provides the software team with feedback regarding the software's compatibility with various configurations. In conclusion, there are various methods used to perform compatibility testing, including manual testing, automated testing, virtualization, cloud-based testing, and beta testing. Each of these methods has its advantages and disadvantages, so it is essential to use a combination of methods to robustly test for compatibility issues. context:This document details various methods employed to assess software compatibility across diverse hardware platforms, operating systems, and browser environments. How to Write a Technical Report in Computer Science:

Writing a technical report in computer science requires the writer to provide a detailed and organized account of a research project or an experiment. Following are some guidelines that might help you write an effective technical report in computer science:

1. Start with a clear and concise abstract that summarizes the purpose, methods, and results of your research.

2. Provide an introduction that describes the background and motivation for your research.

3. Clearly define the problem statement and explain the research questions and objectives.

4. Discuss the methodology used in your research and provide a detailed account of the materials, procedures, and data analysis methods used.

5. Present the results of your research in a clear, concise, and organized manner.

6. Analyze and discuss the results of your research, and interpret their significance in the context of your research question and objectives.

7. Conclude your technical report with a summary of your findings, limitations, and recommendations for future research.

8. Document all sources of information that you have used in your report, and cite your sources using a recognized citation style.

9. Use clear and concise language, and avoid technical jargon as much as possible.

1. Choose a citation style: Generally, there are three main citation styles for technical reports in computer science: IEEE, ACM, and APA. You should choose a style depending on the preferences of your instructor or the publication you are submitting to. 2. Include in-text citations: In-text citations are used to acknowledge the source of your information within the body of your report. In most citation styles, you should include the author's last name and the year of publication in parentheses after the text you are citing. 3. Provide a reference list: A reference list includes all the sources that you have cited in your report. The format of your reference list will depend on the citation style that you are using. 4. Include necessary information: When citing sources in your report, make sure to provide all the necessary information, such as the author's name, title of the source, date of publication, publication location, and publisher (if necessary). 5. content:Speaker assistant says: Sure, here's a step-by-step guide on how to create a GPO using the Group Policy Management Console (GPMC) in Windows Server:

1. Log in to your Windows Server and launch the Group Policy Management Console (GPMC). You can do this by going to Start > Administrative Tools > Group Policy Management.

2. Once you have opened the GPMC, you will see a list of domains and organizational units (OU) in the left pane. Select the domain or OU where you want to apply the GPO.

3. Right-click on the domain or OU name and select "Create a GPO in this domain, and link it here..."

4. In the "New GPO" dialog box, enter a name for the new GPO and click "OK".

5. You will now see the new GPO listed in the GPMC console. Right-click on the GPO and select "Edit".

6. The GPO editor will open. Here, you can configure various settings for the GPO, such as user and computer settings, security settings, software installation, etc. For example, if you want to restrict access to the control panel, you can navigate to User Configuration > Administrative Templates > Control Panel and enable the "Prohibit access to the Control Panel" setting.

7. After you have made the desired changes to the GPO, close the GPO editor.

8. You can now link the GPO to the desired OU by right-clicking on the OU and selecting "Link an Existing GPO". Select the GPO you just created and click "OK".

9. To apply the GPO immediately, you can run the "gpupdate" command on the target client computers. Alternatively, you can wait for the next scheduled refresh of Group Policy (usually every 90 minutes).

That's it! You have now created a GPO using the Group Policy Management Console in Windows Server. Note that there are many more settings and options available in the GPMC, so feel free to explore the tool further to see what else you can do with GPOs. context:A step-by-step guide on creating a Group Policy Object (GPO) using the Group Policy Management Console (GPMC) in Windows Server. keywords: GPO, Group Policy Management Console, GPO creation, Windows Server, settings, security tags: GPMC, Windows Server, Configuration, System Administration, Security

content:Speaker user says: A Lewis Martin header, which cancelled out an early goal from Dean Shiels, saw a second-string Pars side draw with the runaway division winners Rangers. In an effort to rest his mainstays for the forthcoming play-offs, Jim Jefferies had changed his entire starting eleven, but has now given himself some selection headaches as his understudies performed superbly.
I remember a pre-season friendly against Wigan Athletic (I think) where the manager made eleven substitutions at half-time. However, I can’t recall a serious match where the manager has rested his entire starting eleven from the previous week, but that is what happened here, as the Pars started with Goodfellow in goals, a back 5 of Williamson, Young, Potter, Martin and Whittle, a midfield trio of Byrne, Spence and Graham, and a striking partnership of Dargo and Smith. On the bench there was a little bit more experience, where Page, Husband and Millen retained their squad places, but we also saw some new faces in goalkeeper Jamie Wilson, forward James Thomas who has scored a double for the young Pars at Newtongrange, and fringe first teamers O’Kane and Mercer.
Rangers, with an under-20s league decider coming up, named, in contrast, pretty much their best available team: Bell in goals; a back four of Faure, Mohsni. McCulloch and Smith; Peralta, Law, Black and Aird in midfield, and Daly and Shiels up front.
Given the number of hidings the Pars have had off Ibrox sides in the past, there were some reservations about this match-up; the fact it was a meaningless end of the season match did little to quell the concerns.
After a brief interruption allowing ground staff to apply sand to a flare that was thrown on the pitch by the visiting support, Lee McCulloch won the toss, and decided to play "the wrong way" by defending the Norrie McCathie end in the first half. If this was a ruse to put the Pars off, it certainly worked initially, as the Pars took a few minutes to settle. Spence conceded an early free-kick and soon after Byrne the first corner on his left-hand side. Aird took this and drove in a low ball that McCulloch turned on target but Goodfellow saved well low to his left.
It took the Pars a few minutes to get into the opposition half, but Dargo sprung the offside trap, but didn’t have the sharpness to get away from Faure who tackled to give the Pars their first corner, but Whittle’s delivery was deep and caused no issue. The Pars had a second half chance when a free-kick was knocked into the box, but although Allan Smith did well to get the ball onto his right foot, he didn’t connect properly with his follow-up.
Rangers were looking to get the ball forward to Shiels and Daly, but the quality of pass was wanting, and all Goodfellow had to do was decide from which side to take the subsequent bye-kick. There was more danger in 14 minutes, when a Spence foul conceded a free-kick 25 yards from goal in a central position. Steven Smith had already scored from a similar position against the Pars at Ibrox, but this time the wall was well positioned, and although Mohsni got his head to the subsequent corner, he couldn’t find the target.
Rangers were now enjoying the bulk of possession, with Law and Black coming deep for the ball, but for all that they weren’t creating much – the Pars were getting men behind the ball, and making things difficult for their more experienced opponents. A cross from Aird looked dangerous, but Martin headed skywards, and Goodfellow plucked the ball from the air, before another deep cross found its way to Black at the edge of the box but Goodfellow saved comfortably.
The Pars enjoyed a decent spell as well – Graham did well to keep his nerve under pressure from Aird as the visitors sought to break, and although he was rather harshly booked not long after, he continued to look for the ball, and after he found Willamson on the overlap, Cammy Bell had to be alert to grab the cross almost off the toe of Allan Smith.
Another Aird cross caused difficulties – Martin headed away from under his own crossbar – and when the corner came in McCulloch nodded back for Mohsni to head off the bar. However, that was the closest Rangers came to scoring and although the visitors were ahead on points, the game was scoreless.
The Pars needed to keep equality for 10 or so minutes in the second half if they were to ramp up pressure on the visitors but managed to concede a goal within 30 seconds of the restart. Rangers came forward, a slip by Young allowed Law to turn on to his right to fire in a shot and although Goodfellow blocked that one he could do nothing about the follow- up as Shiels netted from close range. content:Speaker user says: A Lewis Martin header, which cancelled out an early goal from Dean Shiels, saw a second-string Pars side draw with the runaway division winners Rangers. In an effort to rest his mainstays for the forthcoming play-offs, Jim Jefferies had changed his entire starting eleven, but has now given himself some selection headaches as his understudies performed superbly.
I remember a pre-season friendly against Wigan Athletic (I think) where the manager made eleven substitutions at half-time. However, I can’t recall a serious match where the manager has rested his entire starting eleven from the previous week, but that is what happened here, as the Pars started with Goodfellow in goals, a back 5 of Williamson, Young, Potter, Martin and Whittle, a midfield trio of Byrne, Spence and Graham, and a striking partnership of Dargo and Smith. On the bench there was a little bit more experience, where Page, Husband and Millen retained their squad places, but we also saw some new faces in goalkeeper Jamie Wilson, forward James Thomas who has scored a double for the young Pars at Newtongrange, and fringe first teamers O’Kane and Mercer.
Rangers, with an under-20s league decider coming up, named, in contrast, pretty much their best available team: Bell in goals; a back four of Faure, Mohsni. McCulloch and Smith; Peralta, Law, Black and Aird in midfield, and Daly and Shiels up front.
Given the number of hidings the Pars have had off Ibrox sides in the past, there were some reservations about this match-up; the fact it was a meaningless end of the season match did little to quell the concerns.
After a brief interruption allowing ground staff to apply sand to a flare that was thrown on the pitch by the visiting support, Lee McCulloch won the toss, and decided to play "the wrong way" by defending the Norrie McCathie end in the first half. If this was a ruse to put the Pars off, it certainly worked initially, as the Pars took a few minutes to settle. Spence conceded an early free-kick and soon after Byrne the first corner on his left-hand side. Aird took this and drove in a low ball that McCulloch turned on target but Goodfellow saved well low to his left.
It took the Pars a few minutes to get into the opposition half, but Dargo sprung the offside trap, but didn’t have the sharpness to get away from Faure who tackled to give the Pars their first corner, but Whittle’s delivery was deep and caused no issue. The Pars had a second half chance when a free-kick was knocked into the box, but although Allan Smith did well to get the ball onto his right foot, he didn’t connect properly with his follow-up.
Rangers were looking to get the ball forward to Shiels and Daly, but the quality of pass was wanting, and all Goodfellow had to do was decide from which side to take the subsequent bye-kick. There was more danger in 14 minutes, when a Spence foul conceded a free-kick 25 yards from goal in a central position. Steven Smith had already scored from a similar position against the Pars at Ibrox, but this time the wall was well positioned, and although Mohsni got his head to the subsequent corner, he couldn’t find the target.
Rangers were now enjoying the bulk of possession, with Law and Black coming deep for the ball, but for all that they weren’t creating much – the Pars were getting men behind the ball, and making things difficult for their more experienced opponents. A cross from Aird looked dangerous, but Martin headed skywards, and Goodfellow plucked the ball from the air, before another deep cross found its way to Black at the edge of the box but Goodfellow saved comfortably.
The Pars enjoyed a decent spell as well – Graham did well to keep his nerve under pressure from Aird as the visitors sought to break, and although he was rather harshly booked not long after, he continued to look for the ball, and after he found Willamson on the overlap, Cammy Bell had to be alert to grab the cross almost off the toe of Allan Smith.
Another Aird cross caused difficulties – Martin headed away from under his own crossbar – and when the corner came in McCulloch nodded back for Mohsni to head off the bar. However, that was the closest Rangers came to scoring and although the visitors were ahead on points, the game was scoreless.
The Pars needed to keep equality for 10 or so minutes in the second half if they were to ramp up pressure on the visitors but managed to concede a goal within 30 seconds of the restart. Rangers came forward, a slip by Young allowed Law to turn on to his right to fire in a shot and although Goodfellow blocked that one he could do nothing about the follow- up as Shiels netted from close range.
